gaps: Monochrome high-contrast grain is a well-established 'arty' look; one unexpected intrusion, such as a colour or a texture break, would make it fully its own.
The lone figure in the last frame is softer and less resolved than the first two frames; hold the same graphic precision through the ending.
Make the subject or point of view more specific, so the striking imagery says something particular rather than a general mood of unrest and isolation.
Compared with A, there is no authored world. Define a premise and characters whose design stays consistent from frame to frame.
Fix the figure integrity. Bodies that dissolve or smear destroy credibility unless the dissolve is the deliberate idea, and if it is, make it controlled and repeated.
Build an arc from cut to cut, with a staging, scale and timing progression, instead of three unrelated atmospheric tableaux.
Anchor it in a specific subject and idea instead of generic dystopian mood; C's fallen-animal tableau shows how specific an image can be
Resolve the figures and staging: readable bodies, deliberate blocking and real choreography between shots
Build real material and light (practical smoke, physical grain from a real source) instead of a uniform film-look filter
tells: Striking graphic world: high-contrast, grainy, film-like monochrome with silhouetted figures fleeing billowing smoke. It recalls archival or riot photography but is plainly stylised, possibly animated or treated.

Every frame works as a poster: a frieze of runners against an explosion of smoke; a top-down diagonal blade of light cutting through a crowd, with long shadows; a lone pale figure isolated in darkness under falling particles.
The choreography moves from collective chaos to an ordered crowd to a solitary figure. It builds and then narrows, which shows strong editorial intent and variety in scale and point of view.
The texture is integral to the look: grain, flecks of light and soft halation give it material weight. The light is the main compositional tool.
No type is visible. Its absence serves the piece, which works on pure image.

The figures are inconsistent and smeared. The lone figure in frame 3 melts into a vertical streak with no anatomy, and the crowd silhouettes in frame 2 have mushy, merging limbs and ambiguous reflections. These are typical artefacts of generative video.
The look is generic 'cinematic AI': grainy monochrome, smoke bursts, a diagonal shaft of light over anonymous silhouettes. The mood stands in for a subject.
There is no specific idea that carries through. Riot smoke, then a crowd in a light beam, then a lone figure is a chain of moody stock situations, not a choreographed sequence.
The grain and dust look applied over the image as a filter, not part of how it was captured. There is no type, and nothing replaces what it might have carried.
Grainy black-and-white 'archival riot/cinematic' look applied as a wash, an atmosphere with no specific subject or point of view

Figures are smeared and anatomically unresolved: the third-frame standing figure melts into a vertical streak, and crowd silhouettes in frame 2 are blobby and duplicated, consistent with AI video generation
Smoke and diagonal light shafts look impressive at a glance, but nothing is staged or choreographed; people drift rather than act
No type; its absence adds nothing and there is no narrative anchor

Miniature, tableau-like world: a small girl in a white shift among scattered fallen animal figures, lit like a stage diorama by one hard pool of top light. That is a specific, uncanny idea, not a stock subject.

The light is motivated and theatrical: a spotlit circle falling off into deep black, then a backlit wall of fog the figure dissolves into. Haze, dust and the earthy ground give it real material depth.

The frames progress clearly: suspended in fog, standing at the still centre of the carnage, then running from a rolling cloud with animals in pursuit. That reads as a real narrative arc with changing camera distance and energy.
The palette is restrained and deliberate: cold grey fog against warm ochre, rust and umber figures. The wide letterbox crops are used with intent.
No type is visible. Leaving it out serves the piece, because the imagery carries it entirely.
gaps: Push the first frame's composition harder: the figure in fog is soft and placed off to one side without much tension, so it doesn't hold as a poster the way C's frames do.
Vary the scale of the motion more; two of the three frames are wide shots of the ground, and an extreme close-up or abrupt change in scale would add rhythm.
Commit further to one graphic signature, as C does with grain and silhouette, so the look is unmistakable beyond 'well-lit miniature'.

tells: Clear, purposeful concept: signing hands become the visual material, mirrored and multiplied into a kaleidoscopic frame around the performer. It is a meaningful idea tied to accessibility and the song, not effect for its own sake.

Consistent monochrome grade, competent studio lighting with a black ground, and in the final frame backlit hair against a grid of practical bulbs. That is professional but conventional music-video lighting.
Performer casting and direction feel real and human. The frames vary between symmetric mirror composites and a tight handheld portrait.
The mirrored-hands composite is a fairly familiar editing trick, and the symmetric framing repeats from frame to frame.
No type is visible. Its absence is neutral, but the idea would have room for type made from signing gestures and leaves that unused.
gaps: Build lighting with texture and a point of view instead of clean studio black; A's single motivated source shows how much atmosphere that adds.
Develop the hand-mirroring device past simple symmetry: change its scale, the timing of the multiplication and its spatial depth so it evolves across the film instead of repeating.
Find one image only this piece could own. Right now it reads as a well-made performance video, not a memorable piece of design.

tells: Competent CG open-movie production: rigged characters (an elderly man, a pink-and-white robot), detailed hard-surface environments, sparks, volumetric fire. This is real studio pipeline work, not template output.
The first frame is a genre key-art collage: a montage of character heads, cyan and magenta rim lights and a logo lockup. It is generic sci-fi poster convention.
Typography is a stock futuristic display face for the title next to a software brand logo. It has no typographic idea.
The palette moves from teal and magenta to orange fire, the standard blockbuster teal-and-orange. The fire close-up of gripping hands shows decent cinematography and texture.
The idea is conventional action sci-fi; the piece doubles as a demo for the software, which dilutes its authorship.
gaps: Replace the genre-default palette and key-art collage with a deliberate visual language that is specific to this story, the way A uses a diorama and C uses graphic monochrome.
Give the title typography a point of view (a custom treatment woven into the world) instead of a stock sci-fi face beside a product logo.
Find a central idea beyond 'old man versus robot in a burning facility': an emotional or formal surprise a juror would remember after the screening.

tells: A specific, strange image: a pale child-like figure standing in a spotlit clearing among fallen, stylised animal bodies. It reads like a fable, and a viewer would remember it.
The light is motivated and theatrical. A single overhead pool falls off into true black, and soft fog in frames 1 and 3 gives the scene atmosphere and depth.
The materials look tactile, like a miniature or stop-motion set: painted animal figures, a dusty ground plane, deliberate grain. It does not have the plastic finish of CG defaults.

The frames show choreography. The film moves from a floating, falling figure lost in mist, to a still central tableau, to a run across the ground with the animals in pursuit and a fog bank rolling in. That is a real narrative arc with changes of scale and tempo.
There is no type, and its absence serves the piece. The images carry the story without any typographic help.
gaps: It is the best of the four, so these gaps are against top-of-year work. Push the scale contrast further, for example an extreme wide that dwarfs the figure, so the world feels larger than one lit set.
The palette is limited to warm ochre on black. Bring in one unexpected colour accent at a key beat to mark the story's turn.
The running frame is less composed than the tableau. Give the climactic action the same graphic precision as the centred spotlight frame.

tells: This is live-action black-and-white music-video photography with real performers, sign-language hands and practical stage lights. It is competently lit, with a rim light on hair and bokeh from the rig.
The idea is clear and humane: signing performers mirrored and kaleidoscoped around a singer. It is legible, but it rests on one mirroring effect.
The mirrored-hands composition repeats across frames 1 and 2 with the subject swapped, which is close to a single layout reused.
Monochrome is a safe default here rather than a palette decision. There is no type to judge, and the piece neither needs nor misses it.
gaps: Compared with A, there is no built world. Give the signing hands an image system of their own, through scale, multiplication or physical staging, instead of a symmetric mirror effect.
The grading is flat, generic black-and-white. Commit to a lighting idea per section, for example hard top light against silhouette, so each frame works as a poster.
Use the gesture as choreography across cuts, with a sign completing from one shot into the next, so the motion has a structure and not just coverage.

tells: This is a full 3D character-animation pipeline: a sculpted old-man hero, a rigged robot, fire simulation and sparks, volumetric haze. That is studio-level production.
Frame 1 is a key-art poster with the software's logo and a generic sci-fi display face in tracked caps. It reads as a showcase thumbnail, not a typographic idea.
The palette is the stock sci-fi split of cyan and magenta against orange fire. The look is genre-default: robot uprising, grizzled hero, burning factory.
The film frames themselves have convincing light and material work, such as the rim-lit robot, ember particles and a warm close-up of fire on hands.
gaps: Compared with A, there is no singular idea. Replace genre shorthand (killer robot, gruff survivor) with an image or premise only this film could own.
The palette is the default cyan, magenta and orange. Choose a restricted, unusual scheme and let light do the storytelling, as A does with one pool of light.
The title and key art are generic. Design a title treatment with a point of view that works with the image, instead of a logo-and-sci-fi-font lockup.

tells: Fully art-directed CG characters with distinct designs (weathered old man, pink-lit android) and real material detail: skin, wool knit, scuffed plastic armour
Motivated, high-contrast lighting: cyan/magenta key art, then sparks and fire practicals, then a warm firelit close-up of clasped mechanical and human hands
The shots move in scale and emotion, from an ensemble poster to a robot in an action pose to an intimate insert, which suggests real editing and choreography
Custom stencil-cut 'CHARGE' title lockup fits the sci-fi world, but it reads as standard key-art branding and does more marketing than typography
gaps: The premise (grizzled hero against a killer robot) is genre-familiar; it needs a stranger, more specific idea like C's tableau of fallen animals
The cyan/magenta-into-orange palette is the stock sci-fi blockbuster grade; a more distinctive colour scheme would make it its own
Title and key art follow game-trailer conventions; give the type a role inside the film rather than a poster lockup

tells: Clear concept: sign language as the visual centre of a music video, with signing hands mirrored and kaleidoscoped around the performers
Monochrome on black isolates hands and faces, and backlit hair and stage lights in the third frame give real photographic depth
Several performers and setups, from symmetric composite to medium shot to backlit close-up, show a planned shoot rather than one repeated layout
No type visible; that suits a piece about non-written language, but nothing is gained from it either
gaps: The mirrored-hands composite is a known effect; push it into choreography that only signing could make
The black-and-white is safe and generic; a lighting or tonal idea specific to this piece would lift it
The frames vary less than they should: two of three are centred subjects on black, so it needs more compositional risk and surprise

tells: A singular, uncanny image: a small pale figure standing in a pool of light among fallen, red-brown animals, a tableau that stays with you
Tactile, miniature/puppet materiality, with real soil, shadows and practical fog, lit like theatre from a single hard top light
Strong progression across frames: a figure dissolving in grey haze, then the overhead tableau, then a low wide chase as fog rolls in, giving clear narrative choreography and changes of scale
Extreme widescreen framing and huge negative space are used on purpose; no type appears, and its absence keeps the piece silent and mythic
gaps: Some darkness crushes detail in the wide shot; protect more readable texture in the shadows
The fog-to-tableau-to-chase arc is strong, but one more surprising formal shift (colour or scale) would push it toward best-of-year
Even if the film itself stays wordless, a title or end-card treatment as considered as the images would complete the package
